But if it is precisely the trial and error before reaching an answer that trains thinking, then this convenience must be called a double-edged sword. Looking things up and thinking are things that look alike but are different. The former is merely collecting information that already exists, while the latter is the work of connecting pieces of information and creating new meaning. Knowledge gained easily is lost easily. Even if it looks like a detour, we must not give up the experience of asking our own questions and searching for answers while unsure.

When people discuss Japanese art, the word 'ma' often comes up: the silence between notes in music, the empty space in painting, the brief pause in conversation. All of these seem to contain nothing, but in fact play an important part in the expression.
If Western aesthetics has found value in filling space, Japanese aesthetics could be said to have entrusted meaning to emptiness. That said, this contrast tends to be an oversimplification. What really matters is that empty space works as a device that draws in the imagination of the audience. By not saying everything, a work begins a dialogue with the person viewing it.

en:
It has long been said that experts' statements are no longer trusted as much as before. Because of the spread of the internet, anyone can send out information, and as a result experts' opinions tend to be seen as just one of many.
That said, experts are not entirely blameless. If they speak with certainty about uncertain matters and later are forced to correct themselves, it is natural that trust is shaken. Perhaps what is really wanted is an attitude of openly showing 'we know this much, but beyond this we don't know'. The honesty to admit what one does not know should, in the long run, become the foundation of trust.

We should be careful about bringing generative AI into schools. The essence of learning lies in the process of facing what you do not understand and reaching understanding by yourself. If AI shows the answer instantly, that process is skipped, and the very ability to learn could be damaged.

Even if AI is shut out of the classroom, students will just use it at home. In that case, it makes more sense to teach how to use it: not to swallow AI's answers whole, but to check the evidence and examine them critically. Isn't teaching that attitude exactly the role of education from now on?

B
{終身雇用|しゅうしんこよう}の{弊害|へいがい}は{否定|ひてい}しない。しかし、{長期|ちょうき}の{雇用|こよう}が{保障|ほしょう}されているからこそ、{企業|きぎょう}は{時間|じかん}をかけて{人材|じんざい}を{育|そだ}て、{社員|しゃいん}は{安心|あんしん}して{技能|ぎのう}を{磨|みが}けるという{面|めん}もある。{制度|せいど}を{一気|いっき}に{捨|す}て{去|さ}るのではなく、その{長所|ちょうしょ}を{生|い}かしつつ{柔軟性|じゅうなんせい}を{高|たか}める{道|みち}を{探|さぐ}るべきだ。
en:
A
Lifetime employment no longer fits the times. Today, when technology changes rapidly, there is no guarantee that skills built at one company will remain useful forever. A society where individuals build their own careers actively and can change jobs when needed is healthier.
B
I do not deny the harms of lifetime employment. But because long-term employment is guaranteed, companies can take time to develop people, and employees can improve their skills with peace of mind. Rather than throwing the system away all at once, we should look for a way to make it more flexible while keeping its strengths.

en:
This is an age that fears boredom. Even in the few minutes waiting for a train, we reach for a screen by reflex. Free time is seen as a blank to be filled, and doing nothing is even thought of as a waste.
But is boredom really useless? Some psychology research reports that creative ideas come more easily after a boring task. When outside stimulation stops, the mind turns inward and begins to freely connect memories and thoughts. Unexpected ideas are probably born from such empty space.
As long as we are always distracting ourselves with something, we keep missing the chance for this inner activity. In modern times, putting up with boredom may require a kind of courage.

en:
It is no exaggeration to say that convenience stores are now part of Japan's social infrastructure. They do not stop at selling food and daily goods; they handle utility payments, package pickups and even the issuing of government documents, and in disasters they become bases for supplying goods.
However, that convenience rests on someone's burden. The staff needed to run 24 hours are always in short supply, and there are many cases of franchise owners forced to work long hours. The fact that in recent years some stores have started to stop late-night opening is probably a sign of this.
Haven't we taken 'always open' too much for granted? If we enjoy convenience, we also need to look at the working conditions of the people who support it.
